procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 03.12.2014 of the High Court
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. Respondents preferred Criminal Miscellaneous No. 12468 of 2014 against the order dated 14.12.2013. The High Court confirmed the order dated 14.12.2013 on 25.03.2014.
2. Respondents preferred Criminal Miscellaneous No. 25561 of 2014 for anticipatory bail. The High Court passed an order on 03.12.2014.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, aggrieved by the High Court's order dated 03.12.2014, appealed to the Supreme Court by way of special leave. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

directions: The respondents are granted four weeks' time from today to surrender before the appropriate court and seek for regular bail.
It is made clear that the present conclusion is confined only to the disposal of this petition and the trial court is free to decide the case on merits.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in granting anticipatory bail to the respondents in the present facts and circumstances of the case?

facts: The respondents were accused of committing offences under the Indian Penal Code and Section 3(1)(xi) of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 (the SC/ST Act).
The High Court granted anticipatory bail to the respondents.
The complainant appealed the High Court's decision to the Supreme Court, arguing that anticipatory bail was not permissible for offences under the SC/ST Act.
law: Section 18 of the SC/ST Act creates a specific bar on the application of Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which is the provision for granting anticipatory bail.
Offences under the SC/ST Act are considered a separate and special class of crimes intended to protect members of Scheduled Castes and Tribes from humiliation, subjugation, and indignity.
The purpose of the bar on anticipatory bail is to prevent accused persons from misusing their liberty to terrorize victims and obstruct a proper investigation.
application: The Supreme Court observed that the complaint contained specific averments that made out a prima facie case against the respondents for an offence under the SC/ST Act.
The Court determined that the respondents' argument that the complaint was false or malicious could not be considered at the bail stage, as such matters are to be decided during the trial.
Since a prima facie case under the SC/ST Act was established, the absolute bar under Section 18 of that Act was triggered.
Consequently, the High Court had no jurisdiction to grant anticipatory bail under Section 438 of the Code.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in granting anticipatory bail because Section 18 of the SC/ST Act creates an absolute bar against it. The Court held that the High Court had committed a "grave error" by granting bail in defiance of this statutory prohibition. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in granting anticipatory bail to the respondents in the present facts and circumstances of the case?
appellant_arguments: The High Court was not justified in granting anticipatory bail, especially considering the factual conclusions reached by the Additional Sessions Judge in the order dated 14.12.2013.
The appellant's counsel pointed to the complaint, the complainant's statement, and the relevant provisions of the SC/ST Act to argue against the grant of bail.
respondent_arguments: The allegations are false, as the appellant was a maid being used to settle scores between respondent No. 1 and his brother due to a long-standing dispute.
Since the High Court granted them anticipatory bail on 03.12.2014, no untoward incident has occurred, and they have cooperated with the investigating officer.
Given the circumstances, the High Court was correct in granting anticipatory bail, and the Supreme Court should not interfere.

cases.case_name: Bachu Das vs. State of Bihar and Others
cases.principle: The provided text states this case was 'followed' by the Court, but does not specify the legal principle for which it was cited.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The provided text does not contain a discernible binding legal rule.
obiter: The Act concerning Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes was enacted because the atrocities committed against them were no longer tolerable.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court's core finding was that the respondents' defense—that the complaint against them was false, malicious, and intended to settle a family dispute—is a matter to be decided at trial, not at the pre-trial stage of considering anticipatory bail. The High Court erred by delving into the merits of this defense when a prima facie case had already been established by the Magistrate and upheld by the Sessions Court.
legal_tests_applied: Whether a prima facie case has been made out against the accused, based on the complaint and statements.
The legal principle that the 'malafide or bona fide of a case can only be taken into consideration at the time of trial' and cannot be examined at the stage of taking cognizance and issuing process.
why_appellant_lost: The respondents' primary argument that the complaint was false and malicious was rejected because the court held that such a plea 'cannot be looked into at the stage of taking cognizance and issue of process and the malajide or bona fide of a case can only be taken into consideration at the time of trial.'
The precedent relied upon by the respondents, Nirmal Jeet Kaur vs. State of M.P. and Another, was held to be inapplicable to the facts of the case.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the appellant's argument by finding that the Magistrate had 'carefully perused the complail)t as well as the.statement of the complainant and arrived at a conclusion that a prima facie case is made against the respondents which was upheld in revision before the Sessions Court.'

The court agreed with the appellant that the High Court was not justified in granting anticipatory bail, particularly in light of the factual conclusions reached by the lower courts, which 'cannot be easily brushed aside by elaborate discussion on the eviderice.'
policy_considerations: The court referred to the Statement of Objects and Reasons of the SC/ST Act, noting that the historical situation for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes 'had been felt not to be tolerable any more, consequently, the present Act was enacted,' thereby emphasizing the legislative intent to treat offenses under this Act with seriousness.
